title: AI Exhaustion
author: Fitzy History
source: Teaching in the Age of AI (fitzyhistory.substack.com), May 18, 2026
summary: Writing at the tired end of the 2025-2026 school year, a history teacher reflects on nine months spent watching the gap between what AI actually is and how schools engage with it grow wider rather than narrower. His central claim: this was the year AI became ambient, unavoidable, and still mostly unaddressed, any student on the internet can reach a frontier model through Google's AI mode, making "forbidding" AI semantic theatre. Schools are finally reacting, often by targeting devices, but their conversations remain anchored in 2023-era AI even as models now build applications and conduct multi-step research. Most meaningfully, AI is forcing existential questions about the purpose of schooling, and it cost him something concrete: he covered less content this year.
points: 2025-2026 is framed as the year AI became ambient, unavoidable, and still mostly unaddressed in schools.
Because any student on the internet can reach a frontier model through Google's AI mode, teachers who claim to "forbid" AI are engaging in "semantic theatre."
Schools are finally reacting, often by restricting devices, but conversations remain stuck in 2023-era AI while models now build apps and run multi-step research.
AI is forcing existential questions about purpose, what schools are for when obtaining and presenting information approaches zero cost.
The transition carried a hidden, anecdotal cost: constant vigilance and in-class assessment meant the author simply covered less content this year.
quotes: the 2025 - 2026 school year will be remembered as the one where AI became ambient, unavoidable, and still mostly unaddressed.
I’ve argued since last June that teachers who claim they “forbid” AI are engaging in semantic theatre once a student is on the internet
Any notion that AI will not have a significant impact on teaching and learning is pure nostalgia.
What are schools actually for when obtaining and presenting information - in virtually any format we require - is approaching zero cost?

the skills hardest to automate are the ones the humanities have always tried to teach: empathy, curiosity, the ability to ask good questions, and the patience to sit with ones that don't have clear answers.

AI has added more monitoring, more in-class assessment, and more rethinking of assignments to a curriculum that was never conceived with it in mind. If schools don't change their approach, something has to give - and right now, for me, it's content.
